claims.text: What the image looks like Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM of MV, dynamic LVOT obstruction → hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
claims.quote: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM of MV, dynamic LVOT obstruction Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

claims.text: Example echocardiogram: a severely thickened ventricular septum and posterior wall of the left ventricle
claims.quote: This echocardiogram shows severely thickened ventricular septum (VS) and posterior wall (PW) of the left ventricle in a patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Wall thickness: septum, posterior wall (>11 mm = LVH)
claims.quote: Wall thickness - septum, posterior wall (>11 mm = LVH).

claims.text: Systolic function (LVEF): HFrEF ≤40% / HFmrEF 41-49% / HFpEF ≥50%
claims.quote: Systolic function (LVEF): HFrEF ≤40% / HFmrEF 41-49% / HFpEF ≥50%.

claims.text: Diagnostic in adults: maximal diastolic LV wall thickness ≥ 15 mm on echo or MRI without another cause; ≥ 13 mm may be used with a family history or a pathogenic sarcomeric variant
claims.quote: In adults, a maximal diastolic left ventricular (LV) wall thickness ≥ 15 mm determined by echocardiography or MRI, in the absence of an alternative cause, is considered diagnostic (1). A lower diagnostic threshold (≥ 13 mm) may be used in patients with a family history of HCM or those with a pathogenic sarcomeric gene variant.

claims.text: Echo quantifies hypertrophy and LVOT obstruction and shows systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and MR severity; obstructive HCM = peak LVOT gradient ≥ 30 mm Hg (≥ 50 mm Hg generally thought sufficient to cause symptoms)
claims.quote: Echocardiography can differentiate HCM from other cardiomyopathies (see figure ), quantify the severity of left ventricular hypertrophy and the degree of left ventricular (LVOT) obstruction, and visualize systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve and the severity of mitral regurgitation (1). Patients are classified as having obstructive HCM if the peak LVOT gradient is ≥ 30 mm Hg (gradients ≥ 50 mm Hg are generally thought sufficient to cause symptoms) (1, 4).

claims.text: Symptoms with an LVOT gradient < 50 mm Hg → provocative maneuvers (eg, Valsalva, exercise echo) to look for latent obstruction
claims.quote: Since the LVOT gradient varies with loading conditions, patients with symptoms and LVOT gradients < 50 mm Hg should undergo provocative maneuvers (eg, Valsalva maneuver, exercise echocardiography) to determine whether latent LVOT obstruction can be elicited (1).

claims.text: ECG frequently shows LVH with repolarization abnormalities (deep T-wave inversions, ST depression); Q waves and LA enlargement are common
claims.quote: The standard 12-lead ECG frequently demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy with repolarization abnormalities, including deep T-wave inversions and ST-segment depression; Q waves and evidence of left atrial enlargement are common.

claims.text: CXR is often normal because the ventricles are not dilated, although LA enlargement may be seen
claims.quote: Chest radiography is often normal because the ventricles are not dilated, although left atrial enlargement may be seen.

claims.text: Causes Most common monogenic cardiac disorder (estimated 1:200 to 1:500 adults); sarcomere gene variants (most often MYBPC3 and MYH7) are found in approximately 35% of those tested
claims.quote: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common monogenic cardiac disorder with an estimated prevalence of 1:200 to 1:500 adults (1). Pathogenic variants encoding elements of the cardiac sarcomere (most frequently MYBPC3 and MYH7) can be detected in approximately 35% of patients with a clinical diagnosis of HCM who undergo genetic testing (2).

claims.text: Most common pattern: asymmetric hypertrophy of the basal interventricular septum; approximately two-thirds have dynamic LVOT obstruction (gradient ≥ 30 mm Hg at rest or with provocation) from the hypertrophied septum plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
claims.quote: The most common morphologic pattern is asymmetric hypertrophy of the basal interventricular septum resulting in reversed septal curvature. However, hypertrophy may affect any LV segment and may be focal or symmetric. Apical HCM is a distinct phenotype characterized by hypertrophy of the distal LV without left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, and it is more commonly observed in individuals of Asian descent (2). Approximately two-thirds of patients with HCM exhibit dynamic LVOT obstruction, defined as a LVOT gradient ≥ 30 mm Hg at rest or with physiologic provocation (3, 4, 5). LVOT obstruction results from an interplay of the hypertrophied basal interventricular septum and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.

claims.text: Systolic function is typically preserved or supranormal, but myocardial stiffness impairs diastolic filling, raising LV end-diastolic and pulmonary venous pressures
claims.quote: Systolic function is typically preserved or supranormal; however, myocardial stiffness leads to impaired diastolic filling, elevated LV end-diastolic pressures, and subsequent increases in pulmonary venous pressures (1).

claims.text: Symptoms A relatively common cause of sudden death in young athletes
claims.quote: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a relatively common cause of sudden death in young athletes (1).

claims.text: Symptoms most commonly appear in the 30s to 50s and are frequently exertional: dyspnea, chest pain (usually like typical angina), palpitations, syncope; often worsened by conditions that reduce preload or afterload and raise heart rate and contractility
claims.quote: Symptoms most commonly manifest in early to mid-adulthood (in patients who are in their 30s to 50s) (3) and are frequently exertional. Typical symptoms include dyspnea, chest pain (usually resembling typical angina), palpitations, and syncope. Exertional symptoms are often exacerbated by physiologic conditions that reduce preload or afterload and increase heart rate and contractility, thereby augmenting dynamic LVOT obstruction.

claims.text: Syncope, particularly exertional, may come from LVOT obstruction or arrhythmia and is an important marker of increased sudden cardiac death risk
claims.quote: Syncope, particularly when exertional, may result from LVOT obstruction or arrhythmia and is an important marker of increased risk for sudden cardiac death (4).

claims.text: Classic murmur: dynamic, late-peaking systolic murmur at the left sternal border (third or fourth intercostal space) that increases with Valsalva or squat-to-stand (less preload) and decreases with handgrip, prolonged squatting or passive leg raise
claims.quote: The classic finding on physical examination is a dynamic, late-peaking systolic murmur, best appreciated along the left sternal border in the third or fourth intercostal space. The intensity of this murmur increases with maneuvers that decrease preload (eg, Valsalva, squat-to-stand) and decreases with maneuvers that increase afterload or preload (eg, hand grip, prolonged squatting, passive leg raise).

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: β-blocker; avoid dehydration / vasodilators; mavacamten / myectomy
claims.quote: β-blocker; avoid dehydration / vasodilators; mavacamten / myectomy

claims.text: Avoid factors that reduce preload or systemic vascular resistance: volume depletion (eg, high-dose diuretics) and systemic vasodilation may worsen obstruction and bring on symptoms
claims.quote: Because LVOT gradients are highly dependent on loading conditions, factors that reduce preload or systemic vascular resistance should be avoided. Volume depletion (eg, from high-dose diuretics) and systemic vasodilation (eg, from vasodilatory medications, post-prandial state, alcohol, elevated ambient temperatures) may exacerbate dynamic obstruction and precipitate symptoms.

claims.text: First line: beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil); avoid verapamil with severe dyspnea at rest, hypotension, an LVOT gradient ≥ 100 mm Hg, or in children < 6 weeks old
claims.quote: First-line pharmacologic therapy consists of beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) (1). These medications decrease heart rate and prolong the diastolic filling interval, thereby augmenting preload, and attenuate LVOT obstruction through their negative inotropic effects. Doses should be titrated to effective relief of symptoms. Verapamil should be avoided in patients with severe dyspnea at rest, hypotension, or a LVOT gradient ≥ 100 mm Hg and in children < 6 weeks of age.

claims.text: Persistent obstruction symptoms (LVOT gradient ≥ 50 mm Hg) despite first-line therapy: consider cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten, aficamten), disopyramide (with an AV nodal blocker), or invasive septal reduction
claims.quote: Patients who continue to experience symptoms related to LVOT obstruction (LVOT gradient ≥ 50 mm Hg) despite first-line medical therapy should be considered for cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten, aficamten), disopyramide (in combination with an atrioventricular nodal blocking agent), or invasive septal reduction therapies (1).

claims.text: Septal reduction therapy for persistent symptomatic LVOT obstruction despite medical therapy including cardiac myosin inhibitors
claims.quote: Septal reduction therapy is performed in patients who have persistent symptomatic LVOT obstruction despite medical interventions including cardiac myosin inhibitors.
